questions.question: Entities come in two distinct groups, and certain cross-group pairs are allowed. Which description fits a bipartite matching of these entities?
options: A set of allowed pairs that together use every entity of both groups exactly once
A set of pairs taken from either group, each entity used in at most one pair
A set of allowed pairs, each with one member of each group, no entity in two pairs
A set of allowed pairs, each with one member of each group, entities may repeat

questions.question: Two groups of entities are drawn as a network: entities are vertices and allowed cross-group pairs are edges. In this picture, which set of edges is a matching?
options: A set of edges that together reach every vertex at least once
A set of edges forming one path through alternate groups
A set of edges in which no two edges share an endpoint
A set of edges that all share one common endpoint

questions.question: Two groups of entities are to be matched, each pair having one member of each group. When is a bipartite matching called perfect?
options: When every entity in the smaller group belongs to one selected pair
When every allowed pair between the two groups has been selected
When no further allowed pair can be added to the selected pairs
When every entity in both groups belongs to exactly one selected pair

questions.question: Why can a perfect bipartite matching exist only when the two groups have the same number of entities?
options: Each pair uses one entity of each group, and every entity must be used once.
Each pair must use two entities of the larger group to balance the sizes.
Larger groups would need more allowed pairs than any network can contain.
Pairs between unequal groups would have to share an endpoint in the network.

questions.question: Which of the following pairing tasks is a bipartite matching problem?
options: Pair six students into three study pairs, any two possible
Pair the four odd-degree vertices of a network with each other
Pair consecutive stops of one delivery route, in route order
Pair machines with jobs, each machine doing at most one job

questions.question: Workers $W_1,W_2,W_3$ and jobs $J_1,J_2,J_3$ have allowed pairs $W_1$–$J_1$, $W_1$–$J_2$, $W_2$–$J_2$, $W_2$–$J_3$, $W_3$–$J_1$, $W_3$–$J_3$. Which set is a bipartite matching?
There are 5 workers and 3 jobs, and every worker may do every job. What is the largest number of pairs a bipartite matching can contain?
options: 3, since each pair uses a different job
5, since each pair uses a different worker
8, one pair for each entity in total
15, one pair for each allowed pair

questions.question: Three machines are matched with five jobs, and the selected pairs use every machine once. Which statement about this matching is correct?
options: It is as large as possible, but it is not a perfect matching.
It is a perfect matching, since every machine is in a pair.
It is not a matching, since two jobs are left without a pair.
It can be enlarged by pairing a used machine with a free job.

questions.question: Three agents $A_1,A_2,A_3$ are to be matched with three tasks $T_1,T_2,T_3$, and every agent may do every task. How many perfect bipartite matchings are there?
options: 9, as there are $3\cdot 3$ allowed pairs
27, as each agent has $3$ task choices
3, as there are $3$ agents to place
6, as $3\cdot 2\cdot 1$ choices remain in turn

questions.question: Nurses $N_1,\dots,N_4$ and shifts $S_1,\dots,S_4$ have allowed pairs $N_1$–$S_1$, $N_1$–$S_2$, $N_2$–$S_3$, $N_3$–$S_3$, $N_4$–$S_2$, $N_4$–$S_4$. The matching $M$ is $N_1$–$S_1$, $N_2$–$S_3$, $N_4$–$S_2$. Which entities does $M$ leave unmatched?
options: $N_3$ only

questions.question: Workers $W_1,W_2$ and jobs $J_1,J_2$ have allowed pairs $W_1$–$J_1$, $W_1$–$J_2$, $W_2$–$J_1$. The matching $\{W_1$–$J_1\}$ cannot be extended by any allowed pair. Is it a largest matching?
options: Yes: a matching that cannot be extended is always a largest one.
Yes: $W_2$ is allowed only $J_1$, so it can never be matched.
No: a largest matching here would need $W_1$ in two pairs.
No: $W_1$–$J_2$ and $W_2$–$J_1$ form a matching of two pairs.

questions.question: Workers $W_1,W_2,W_3$ and jobs $J_1,J_2,J_3$ are drawn as a network. The selected edges are $W_1$–$J_1$, $W_2$–$J_1$ and $W_3$–$J_3$. Counting selected edges at each vertex, what can be concluded?
options: A matching, as each worker is an endpoint of one selected edge
A perfect matching, as there are three edges for three workers
Not a matching: $J_1$ is an endpoint of two selected edges
A matching, though not perfect, as $J_2$ has no selected edge

questions.question: Workers $W_1,W_2,W_3$ and jobs $J_1,J_2,J_3$ have allowed pairs $W_1$–$J_1$, $W_2$–$J_1$, $W_3$–$J_1$, $W_3$–$J_2$, $W_3$–$J_3$. The groups are equally large. Does a perfect matching exist?
options: Yes: equal group sizes always allow a perfect matching.
No: $W_1$ and $W_2$ both need $J_1$, so one stays unmatched.
Yes: $W_3$ may take any job, so it can resolve every conflict.
No: $J_2$ and $J_3$ have only one allowed worker each.

questions.question: Four points $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$ must be split into two pairs, any two points may be paired, and the pair costs are PQ 1, RS 1 and 5 for every other pair. A planner first splits the points into the groups $\{P,Q\}$ and $\{R,S\}$ and solves a bipartite matching between them. What is the result?
options: The best split-based pairing costs 10, against 2 without the split.
The best split-based pairing costs 2, the same as without the split.
The split-based problem has no pairing at all, so it is infeasible.
The best split-based pairing costs 10, which is also the true optimum.

questions.question: Workers $W_1,\dots,W_4$ and jobs $J_1,\dots,J_4$ have allowed pairs $W_1$–$J_1$, $W_1$–$J_2$, $W_2$–$J_2$, $W_2$–$J_3$, $W_3$–$J_3$, $W_3$–$J_4$, $W_4$–$J_4$, $W_4$–$J_1$. How many perfect matchings are there?
options: 16, as each worker has 2 allowed jobs, $2^4$
2, as the first choice for $W_1$ fixes every other pair
24, as there are $4\cdot3\cdot2\cdot1$ complete assignments
4, as each job could be the one taken by $W_1$
